explanations.answer: No dew or rain except at his word
explanations.explanation: Elijah says to Ahab, king of Israel, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1) My big announcements are usually “the cookies are DONE,” and even those make me nervous, friend. This one is about the whole sky.

explanations.answer: No harvest until Ahab tears down his altar
explanations.explanation: Elijah never brings up an altar here. His words to Ahab, Israel's king, are about the sky: “…neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1) A harvest answer sounds close, since it's the same kind of trouble. But the text keeps to dew and rain, and I'm going to keep to the text.

explanations.answer: An army will soon surround Samaria
explanations.explanation: No army shows up in Elijah's message to Ahab, Israel's king. He talks about the weather, and only the weather: “…neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1) A drought is a strange thing to announce to a king, but that's what Elijah announces. Soldiers aren't part of it.

Not by Baal. Elijah says, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand…” (1 Kings 17:1) He swears by the LORD, standing in front of a king who serves Baal (1 Kings 16:31). That oath names the LORD, the God of Israel, and nobody else.

False, and the oath tells you why. Elijah says, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand…” (1 Kings 17:1) He swears by the LORD, not by Baal. Ahab serves Baal, a false god (1 Kings 16:31), so Elijah is swearing by a very different name right in front of him.

Ravens it is. The LORD says, “…I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” (1 Kings 17:4) Elijah drinks from the brook, and the birds handle the food. Birds on delivery duty, friend, and some of my packages can't manage that.

Doves are a lovely guess. Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like a dove, so I'm biased. But the LORD says, “…I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” (1 Kings 17:4) The birds on this job are ravens.

Eagles sound like the big, important bird for a big, important job. But the LORD says, “…I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” (1 Kings 17:4) Ravens get the call, not eagles. I would have picked the eagle too, to be honest.

Yes, morning and evening. “The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening…” (1 Kings 17:6) That's two deliveries a day, and the food is bread and meat. The brook covers the drinking.

The text says otherwise. “The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening…” (1 Kings 17:6) So the food comes in the morning and again in the evening, not just once. The brook covers the drinking, so the statement is True.

explanations.answer: There's been no rain in the land
explanations.explanation: The text says it plainly: “…the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.” (1 Kings 17:7) Elijah's own words to Ahab were about no rain (1 Kings 17:1). So the drought he announced reaches even the brook he's living by.

No dam in this story. The text gives one reason: “…the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.” (1 Kings 17:7) Ahab's men aren't mentioned at the brook at all. It's the drought doing it.

No earthquake is mentioned anywhere in this passage. The text gives one reason: “…the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.” (1 Kings 17:7) Sometimes the plain answer is the right answer, friend. Not every story needs a dramatic soundtrack.

A widow. The LORD says, “Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” (1 Kings 17:9) After ravens, it's a person this time, in Zarephath of Sidon. That's a big change in delivery drivers.

Elijah doesn't get sent to a priest. The LORD says, “Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” (1 Kings 17:9) A priest sounds like a fine host, but the text names a widow. Priests never come up in Zarephath at all.

No king in Zarephath here. The LORD says, “Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” (1 Kings 17:9) Elijah just spoke to a king in verse 1, and now he's heading to a widow's door. I think that's about as far from a palace as you can get.

explanations.answer: A little water in a cup
explanations.explanation: Water first. Elijah says, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” (1 Kings 17:10) It's a small ask, and a polite one, with that “please” right there. I think a cup of water means a lot after a dried-up brook. The bread comes a moment later as a second ask.

explanations.answer: A place to stay the night
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask for a bed. The first thing out of his mouth is, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” (1 Kings 17:10) The text doesn't record him asking for a place to stay. Just a drink, then a second ask about bread.

No directions to the elders here. At the city gate, Elijah says, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” (1 Kings 17:10) He's talking to the widow, just as the LORD said a widow would be there (1 Kings 17:9). City elders never come up in this passage.

Yes. Elijah says, “Please bring me a piece of bread.” (1 Kings 17:11) She's already on her way for the water when he calls after her. I've done that to people in my bakery, and I'm still sorry about it.

He does ask. As the widow goes for the water, Elijah calls to her, “Please bring me a piece of bread.” (1 Kings 17:11) So the water is only half the order. And that bread request sets up what she says next.

Flour is right. She says she has “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) A HANDFUL, friend. I've dropped more than that on my apron before breakfast. And she has a son to feed too.
Oil goes in the jug. She says, “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) A little oil, not a full jug. Flour and oil are the whole list.

Honey sounds sweet, but it's not on her list. She says, “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) Honey would make a fine cookie, I'll give you that, but she doesn't mention any. The two things she names are flour and oil.
Wine isn't what's in her jug. She says, “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) So the jug has oil and the jar has flour. Wine never enters the conversation.

Salt doesn't make her list. She says, “…only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.” (1 Kings 17:12) A pinch of salt is useful in a cookie, I'll admit. But she names only flour and oil.

That's what she says. She's gathering sticks to take home and “…prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.” (1 Kings 17:12) I think this is one of the lowest moments in her story. Elijah answers her with “Do not be afraid…” (1 Kings 17:13).

It's true, and it's a heavy thing to say out loud. She says she's gathering sticks “…to take home and prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.” (1 Kings 17:12) Those are her own words about what she has. Elijah answers her with “Do not be afraid…” (1 Kings 17:13).

explanations.answer: Make him a small cake of bread
explanations.explanation: Elijah says, “…first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me.” (1 Kings 17:13) Then she makes some for herself and her son afterward. A small cake, from what she already has.

explanations.answer: Pour him some of her oil
explanations.explanation: Oil isn't what he asks for. He says, “…first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me.” (1 Kings 17:13) The ask is for a cake of bread, made by her, not a pour from the jug. Afterward, she's to make some for herself and her son.

explanations.answer: Give him the flour to keep
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask her to hand over the flour. He says, “…first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me.” (1 Kings 17:13) She does the baking herself. Afterward, she's to make some for herself and her son, and honestly, I'd rather someone ask me for one cookie than my whole bag of flour.

explanations.answer: The LORD says her flour and oil will last until He sends rain
explanations.explanation: Because the LORD says so. Elijah tells her, “…for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’…” (1 Kings 17:14) Elijah isn't promising on his own. The promise comes from the LORD, and the end date is the rain.

explanations.answer: The ravens will keep bringing her food until the rain
explanations.explanation: The ravens aren't part of this promise. Elijah says the LORD promises her jar of flour won't be exhausted and her jug of oil won't run dry until He sends rain (1 Kings 17:14). The ravens fed Elijah at the brook (1 Kings 17:4). The text doesn't send them to Zarephath.

explanations.answer: Her neighbors will share what they have until the rain
explanations.explanation: Neighbors aren't part of Elijah's promise. He says the LORD will keep her flour jar from being exhausted and her oil jug from running dry until the day He sends rain (1 Kings 17:14). The food comes from her own jar and jug. Nobody has to start a group chat.

The text says the opposite. After she follows Elijah's word, “…there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household.” (1 Kings 17:15) The widow's household is right there in that list. Nobody is left out of that sentence.

False. After she follows Elijah's word, “…there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household.” (1 Kings 17:15) The jar of flour and the jug of oil don't run out (1 Kings 17:16). Elijah and her whole household eat, day after day.

explanations.answer: If he came to remind her of her sin
explanations.explanation: She starts with “O man of God…” and then asks, “Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” (1 Kings 17:18) I think this one hurts, friend. The text doesn't tell us why she thinks of her iniquity.

explanations.answer: Why the LORD let the drought go on
explanations.explanation: That's not her question. She asks, “what have you done to me? Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” (1 Kings 17:18) Her words are about her son and what Elijah's visit means to her. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly: the drought isn't what she brings up.

explanations.answer: If he would leave her house for good
explanations.explanation: She doesn't ask him to leave. Her words are “what have you done to me? Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” (1 Kings 17:18) And instead of leaving, Elijah says, “Give me your son.” (1 Kings 17:19) I think that's a hard moment, and Elijah stays in it.

explanations.answer: A widow who has opened her home to him
explanations.explanation: He cries out, “…have You also brought tragedy on this widow who has opened her home to me, by causing her son to die?” (1 Kings 17:20) Elijah names what she did: she opened her home to him. He's speaking straight to the LORD, honest and direct. I think he's hurting right along with her.

explanations.answer: A widow who has asked him to leave her home
explanations.explanation: She doesn't ask him to go in this passage. Elijah describes her as “…this widow who has opened her home to me…” (1 Kings 17:20) He's talking about her welcome, not about her pushing him out. And he's staying in her upper room (1 Kings 17:19).

explanations.answer: A widow who has fed everyone in Zarephath
explanations.explanation: Elijah doesn't say anything about the whole town. He describes her as “…this widow who has opened her home to me…” (1 Kings 17:20) The care he names is for him, in her own house. That's one widow and one open door.

Life. Elijah stretches himself out over the boy three times and cries out, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21) Simple words, big ask. And the boy had no breath remaining in him (1 Kings 17:17), so this is exactly what the moment needs.

Sight isn't what Elijah asks for. He cries out, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21) The boy had no breath remaining in him (1 Kings 17:17), so Elijah's prayer is for life itself. Nothing in the text asks about his eyes.

Voice isn't the word in Elijah's prayer. He cries out, “…please let this boy’s life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21) The boy had no breath remaining in him (1 Kings 17:17). Asking for life covers all of it.

Yes, friend, it's true. “And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived.” (1 Kings 17:22) The LORD listens, and the boy lives. That's the whole sentence, and it's enough to make me hop on my gold base.

The text says the opposite. “And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived.” (1 Kings 17:22) The boy who had no breath remaining in him (1 Kings 17:17) lives. That's the answer to Elijah's prayer.

The text says she's sure. She tells Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth.” (1 Kings 17:24) “Now I know…” doesn't leave much room for doubt. Her son is back in her arms (1 Kings 17:23), and she says it plainly.

False. She says, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth.” (1 Kings 17:24) Earlier she asked what Elijah had done to her (1 Kings 17:18). Now she says she knows. That's a big turn.
